To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the temporal variability of the IFN response upon viral PAMP recognition results mainly from the stochasticity of RIG-I activation and that this heterogeneity is amplified by the stochasticity of NF- κ activation.
stochastic events at early steps of antivival signaling are the origin for the temporal heterogeneity of the entire antiviral response in a single cell.
the IFN system is characterized by a large extent of stochasticity and heterogeneity that results from the stochastic nature of RIG-I activation and the subsequent signaling events.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the stochastic nature of the antiviral response on the single cell level.
the understanding of the dynamics of antipathogen response on single cell level and the identification of key steps in the signaling cascade that determine the efficiency of antiviral immune defense.
the dynamics of antifungal and antiviral immunity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stochastic nature of RIG-I signaling is a key determinant for the dynamics of IFN production.
stochasticity of PAMP signaling is a limiting factor in the antiviral defense and that it is not a consequence of stochasticity of IFN-stimulus.
the IFN system is a highly dynamic system with a high extent of heterogeneity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stochastic nature of RIG-I activation and subsequent signaling is the major source of the heterogeneity of IFN induction.
IFN induction and ISG expression are stochastic processes on the cellular level.
the stochasticity of the RIG-I signaling cascade is a limiting step for the efficiency of IFN induction in the early antiviral response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IFN system is a highly dynamic system and that the heterogeneity of the individual cell response is a major determinant of the outcome of the immune response.
the dynamics of antiretroviral protection are based on stochastic decisions that are not fully predictable.

single-cell analysis of the antiviral defense system reveals a high degree of heterogeneity that is not only based on cell-to-cell variability but is also based on temporal variability within the individual cell.
